title: Spillover provisioning and staged hardware swap — runbook prototype
content:
Context and intent:
This doc is a pragmatic runbook prototype to handle: (A) urgent replacement of a failed accelerator/PCI card on a node, (B) controlled cordon/drain of nodes during partial-failure or maintenance windows, (C) short-term cluster spillover (temporary capacity add) to protect latency SLOs, and (D) steps to recover cluster health and validate correctness post-swap. The focus here is on minimizing user-impact for inference workloads (low tail latency, KV cache preservation where possible) while giving SREs a lightweight, repeatable checklist.

Scope/narrowing assumptions:
- Applies to hosted + dedicated clusters running the Redwood serving runtime with K8s node pools per accelerator family.
- Assumes access to: kubectl (k8s), internal runbooks for hardware swap (rack-level), and the control-plane console.
- We intentionally favor graceful degradation (spillover to lower-capacity pools or quantized model variants) over hard failover where possible.

Quick decision rubric (triage):
- DETECT: Alert types that trigger this flow: sudden spike in pod restart rate, node Ready->NotReady, physical monitor: hw-fault alerts, sustained p99 latency > SLO for 5m with increased queue length.
- SEVERITY 1 (P0): Total loss of >10% cluster GPU capacity or p99 latency >3x SLO for >10m. Trigger incident lead, consider emergency capacity injection.
- SEVERITY 2 (P1): Single-node GPU failures impacting <10% capacity, or one zone degrade. Treat via staged replacement and cordon/drain.

High-level play (summary):
1) Triage & comms: claim incident, post to #sre-urgent and incident channel, notify on-call HW engineer.
2) Protect traffic: move critical routes to higher priority lanes or compatible model variants; enable short-lived autoscale ups on Dedicated if reserve capacity is available.
3) Cordon & drain strategy: pick nodes for drain that maximize KV cache locality preservation.
4) Hardware swap: follow physical-swap checklist; mark node as maintenance, bring up new driver/firmware, validate.
5) Reintroduce node: kube uncordon + pod readiness checks; observe 30–60m for regressions.

Detailed steps (playbook):
A. Initial triage (first 0–10 minutes)
- Run quick cluster checks:
  - kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep -E "NotReady|SchedulingDisabled"
  - kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep -i taint
  - Check serving-runtime dashboards: token queue length, per-route p99/p999, active KV cache hit-rate.
- If p99 > SLO * 2 and queue length trending up: escalate to P0.
- Post status: incident start message with hypothesis and affected pools (copy to incident timeline).

B. Short-term protective actions (10–30 minutes)
- Apply traffic reroutes in control plane: shift sensitive routes to a fallback model (e.g., quantized-variant or lower-context-length model) with a feature-flagged rollout. Use console or API to set route policy to "route: high_priority -> dedicated_pool_a; low_priority -> fallback_pool".
- If Dedicated reserve is available, instant-scale: call autoscale API to add X GPUs into the affected pool (prefer hot-spare nodes). Document call id.
- If no autoscale, enable request-throttling on non-critical routes to preserve capacity for critical traffic.

C. Selecting nodes for cordon/drain (when doing replacement)
- Goal: minimize rewarm penalty for KV cache and maintain latency SLOs.
- Prefer nodes with lowest active-KV population. Use metrics query: sum(kv_entries{node="<node>"})
- Prefer nodes in the same rack to keep cross-rack network impact minimal if rebalancing is required.
- Choose at most 1 node per shard/placement group simultaneously unless capacity permits more.

D. Cordoning and draining (safe flags)
- Mark node unschedulable: kubectl cordon <node> # adds NoSchedule
- Start drain with grace and deletion-timeout tuned for our pod types: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector="app=redwood-serving" --grace-period=60 --timeout=20m
- Watch for stuck pods: kubectl get pods -n serving --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'
- If a pod refuses to evict due to local-storage, consider ephemeral cache snapshot + copy to new node (see cache-handbook).

E. Hardware swap checklist (physical / remote ops)
- Confirm node id, rack, serial numbers match CMDB.
- Power down according to safe-host procedures (or hot-swap if cartridge supports it).
- Remove bad accelerator, replace with tested spare from rack 3 or pool B (document spare id).
- Apply firmware/drivers baseline: verify driver version matches approved list: nvidia-driver-540.x or internal optimized runtime.
- Health checks after swap: lspci | grep NVIDIA ; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,temperature --format=csv
- Reboot if drivers required; annotate maintenance ticket with steps & elapsed time.

F. Reintroduce & validation (post-swap)
- Remove taint/maintenance annotation in CMDB and Kubernetes: kubectl uncordon <node>
- Confirm kubelet re-registers and pods schedule: kubectl get pods -o wide --watch -n serving --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- Post-scheduling checks for serving pods:
  - Health endpoint check: curl -f http://<pod-ip>:8080/health/live && curl -f http://<pod-ip>:8080/health/ready
  - Sample inference smoke test: curl -X POST http://<pod-ip>:8080/generate -d '{"prompt":"hello"}' | jq '.choices'
- Monitor the following 60 minutes: p50/p95/p99 latency, KV cache hit-rate, token CPU/GPU utilization. Rollback if p99 spikes > pre-incident baseline by >25%.

G. Spillover capacity (if triggered)
- If cluster cannot meet SLO with local fixes, spin up spillover pool: create a temporary node-pool with compatible accelerator type or lower-cost accelerators and route low-priority traffic there.
- Prefer warm images (pre-baked with runtime and model variants) to reduce startup time.
- Update routing policy to send best-effort or long-response requests to spillover. Ensure secrets and model weights are synced to pool (rsync or object-store prefetch).
- Track cost: annotate incident with expected $/hr of spillover pool.

H. Partial-degraded mode considerations
- Some inference workloads are sensitive to prompt-prefix caching; if we cannot preserve cache, prefer routing to the same node family to allow KV reuse.
- For stateful workloads, enable sticky session routing where possible until rewarm completes.

I. Post-incident and verification (1–4 hours)
- Run full regression tests against representative prompt set. Compare token-level quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE analogs, hallucination rate) against baseline.
- Reconcile capacity used and costs from console.
- Fill incident timeline with timestamps and decisions.
- Start a short post-incident review (owner + SRE + HW ops): what failed, root cause hypothesis, what worked, what didn’t.

Short checklist (for on-call pocket card):
- [ ] Claim incident and set channel
- [ ] Snapshot cluster node statuses + affected pods
- [ ] Apply protective routing or enable spillover pool
- [ ] Select and cordon drain nodes conservatively (1 at a time)
- [ ] Swap hardware following HW ops guide, confirm drivers
- [ ] Uncordon, smoke-test, observe 60m
- [ ] Run regression suite, cost reconciliation, doc timeline

Known risks and open questions (TODOs):
- KV cache migration story is still fragile: need small tool to snapshot and replay high-frequency prefixes to new node.
- Need exact safe timeouts for drains for different model sizes (gpt-large vs gpt-xxl) — run experiments to tune --grace-period and --timeout.
- Spillover pool image creation: automate prefetch of model shards and runtime in <5m. Today startup is often 10–15m.
- Investigate automated automated rollback triggers (p99 + error-rate combined) to un-schedule newly reintroduced nodes if they regress.

Postmortem prompts to answer when incident closed:
- What was the proximate hardware failure and are there patterns with vendor/firmware?
- How long between detection and traffic protection?
- What was the cache rewarm penalty (tokens/sec) and could it be reduced?
- What is the estimated avoidable customer impact ($ and requests) and what mitigations would have prevented it?
- Action items (owners + dates) for tool automation and HW spare placement.

Appendix — quick commands and queries:
- node status: kubectl get nodes -o wide
- node describe: kubectl describe node <node> | egrep -i "Taint|Condition|Address"
- pods on node: kubectl get pods -n serving --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60 --timeout=20m
- uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>
- smoke test: curl -X POST http://<pod-ip>:8080/generate -d '{"prompt":"sanity"; "max_tokens":8}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json'

Notes-to-self / in-progress items:
- Run controlled experiments next week to measure drain timeout sensitivity (Priya + Miguel).
- Prototype a small KV snapshot tool (Ethan) — integrate with cache-handbook.
- Coordinate with HW to consolidate spare distribution (Sophie).

End of prototype runbook. This should be treated as a living doc — add concrete postmortem-derived actions and convert TODOs into tracked tickets before promoting to "v1".
